title: 691030299514/541NV17: Hsbc Bank Plc 34, Bethcar Street, Ebbw Vale, NP23 6HQ
text:
TRIBIWNLYS PRISIO CYMRU  -  VALUATION TRIBUNAL FOR WALES

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 1 of 10

Appellants: Mr G Bond (Owner) & Mr S Roberts (Occupier)

Appellant’s Address: HSBC Bank, 34 Bethcar Street, Ebbw Vale NP23 6HQ

Appeal number: 691030299514/541NV17/2

The Matter Appealed against: 2017 Rating List

Date of Hearing: 24 September 2019

Appearances: Mr Bond & Mr Roberts
Mr M Pearson for the respondent Valuation Officer (VO)

Date of Decision: 22 October 2019

Decision of Tribunal: Appeal Allowed in Part

Members of the Tribunal: Mrs C Uzzell (Chair), Mrs K Thomas & Mr J C
Alexander

Tribunal Clerk: Mrs S Gwilliam

Introduction:
1. Mr Bond contended, in a proposal to alter an entry in the 2017 Rating List
received by the VO on 3 January 2018, that the Rateable Value (RV) of  the
appeal hereditament was inaccurate and should be reduced from £12,250
to £8,000 RV with effect from the 1 April 2017, for the following reasons:
“The property has been renovated Air Conditioning now removed and
classification as Bank and Premises has now changed to Shop Retail
Restaurant Premises”.
2. Upon the request of the Appellants and with the agreement of the Tribunal,
Mr Pearson presented his case first.
3. This is a summary of the case and is not intended to be an exhaustive record
of the proceedings. However, the parties can be assured that all the
evidence was fully considered by the Tribunal when it arrived at its decision.
Consequently, the absence or reference to any statement, or evidence,
should not be construed as being overlooked.

Summary of the Case
4. Mr Pearson described the subject property as a two-storey former bank
premises currently operating as a shop on the ground floor and storage in
the basement.  As the property was previously occupied by HSBC, he
described the property as a purpose built bank construction as opposed to
a traditional shop.  It is in in the popular high street location of Bethcar Street

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 2 of 10
in Ebbw Vale which adjoins Market Street, the other main high street in the
area.
5. The VO explained that the following issues had been agreed between the
parties prior to the hearing:
• the total net internal area (NIA) of 149.51m2;
• the removal of HSBC from the name of the hereditament;
• the mode or category of use as Shop and Premises;
• the removal of air conditioning units;
• £6,000 pa headline rent for the appeal property effective from the 1
February 2018.
6. Therefore, the only issue in dispute was the rate per metre (£m2) applied to
the valuation at £140m2.
7. The VO explained that the basis of valuation for the appeal property is
defined under Paragraph 2(1) Schedule 6 of the Local Government Finance
Act 1988 (LGFA 1988) as –
2(1) The rateable value of a non-domestic hereditament [none of which
consists of domestic property and none of which is exempt from non-
domestic rating] shall be take to be an amount equal to the rent at which it
is estimated the hereditament might reasonably be expected to let from
year to year on these three assumptions-
(a) the first assumption is that the tenancy begins on the day by reference
to which the determination is to be made;
(b) the second assumption is that immediately before the tenancy begins
the hereditament is in a state of reasonable repair, but excluding from
this assumption any repairs which a reasonable landlord would consider
uneconomic;
(c) the third assumption is that the tenant undertakes to pay all usual
tenant’s rates and taxes and to bear the cost of the repairs and
insurance and the other expenses (if any) necessary to maintain the
hereditament in a state to command the rent mentioned above.
8. The Antecedent Valuation Date (AVD) is specified as the 1st April 2015
under Paragraph 2(3)(b) of Schedule 6 of the LGFA 1988, as the day by
reference to which the rateable value of non-domestic hereditaments are
to be determined for the purposes of the local and central non-domestic
rating lists which were compiled for Wales on the 1st April 2017.
9. In accordance with the case of Lotus and Delta v Culverwell (VO) &
Leicester City Council (1976), the VO clarified that the headline rent of
£6,000 pa, which analysed to circa £74m2, was effective on the 1 February
2018, nearly three years after the AVD and had no defined tenure or terms.
As a result, he was of the view that this rental evidence held little weight.

12. Based on the evidence he had provided, Mr Pearson considered that the
best rental evidence was that which most closely matches the definition of
RV.  From the information available, he considered that a rate of £105m2
is the most appropriate.  In addition, he maintained that settlement evidence
also supported a rate of £105m2 being ascribed, particularly as there were
settlements at higher rates nearby.
13. In relation to the Appellants’ argument concerning the rate per £m2 adopted
for 55 Bethcar Street at £86m2 and 32 Bethcar Street at £80m2, the VO
explained that these properties were both significantly larger than the
appeal property and therefore less comparable.  He clarified that the
subject property had a total area of 149m2 and ITMS 80m2; 32 Bethcar
Street had a total area of 1349.2m2 and ITMS 199.41m2 and 55 Bethcar
Street had a total area of 493m2 and ITMS 150m2.  Therefore, the
valuations applied to these larger units reflected the size differential as
lower rental bids are expected in the market for larger properties.
14. He also maintained that whilst 55 Bethcar Street had been valued in line
with its subject rent, that rent was further from the AVD than other rental
evidence and had to be significantly adjusted as it was let as a shell unit
only and received a significant rent free period.
15. As the rents reflected those shops with standard shop frontages, the VO
stated a non-standard frontage allowance was required as the subject
property has a traditional bank frontage.  A comparable bank with a non-
standard frontage allowance of 10% was ascribed to 14/15 Market Street,
Ebbw Vale and this allowance was in line with the allowances
recommended by the Inter Banking Forum for this frontage type.  Therefore,
Mr Pearson considered a 10% frontage allowance was appropriate for the
subject property as opposed to 7.5% previously ascribed.
16. Based upon the rental and settlement evidence, the VO considered that a
rate of £105m2 was justified which resulted in a valuation of £8,500 RV.
Consequently, Mr Pearson requested that the Tribunal allow the appeal in
part and confirm £8,500 RV for 34 Bethcar Street, Ebbw Vale with effect
from the 1 April 2017.
17. In response to questions, the VO stated:
• The term ITMS stands for In Terms of Main Space.  Zone A is the
most valuable area valued at 100%, Zone B at 50% and the

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 6 of 10
basement as a storage area at 10%.  The toilets appear within the
valuation they are valued at £0;
• The property was measured on NIA (Net Internal Area) and in
accordance with the RICS Measuring Practice, non-structural walls
are measured through, therefore the ornate porch area was included
within the valuation;
• For the 2017 Rating List, the value per £m2 is based on annual rental
values from the AVD of 1 April 2015;
• In relation to the frontage he valued the property – ‘rebus sic
stantibus’ - as it stands and the property is currently used as a shop.
As the property does not have a typical shop frontage, Mr Pearson
considered that the previous allowance was insufficient and
increased it to 10%;
• A national rating agent did not question the £m2 attributed to 10/12
Bethcar Street at £160m2 but sought an allowance for layout and
frontage.  Mr Pearson considered that this property was located in a
better position.
18. Mr Roberts clarified that the shop is his wife’s business and for several
years she operated a market stall throughout the Gwent area.  In the past,
the market in Ebbw Vale was very popular with limited plots available,
however nowadays you are now able to choose your plot.
19. Mrs Roberts originally rented another property, 14 Bethcar Street, but as
the rent was high she vacated this property and rented the appeal
hereditament.
20. Mr Roberts provided the Tribunal with a copy of his presentation which
included several internal and external photographs of the subject property
and a written submission, extracts of which are below:
21. Mr Roberts explained that he believed the £m2 should be reduced to
£80m2, or less, in line with 32 Bethcar Street, a shop located adjacent to
the subject property and which has the benefit of a traditional shop frontage.
This, he stated would equate to £6,400 RV.
22. In addition, the Appellant argued that as Mrs Roberts is paying a rent of
£6,000 pa to Mr Bond, the comparable RV should be circa £6,000.
23. Mr Roberts informed the Tribunal that Blaenau Gwent and Ebbw Vale is at
the top of the list for WIMD (Welsh Index of Multiple Deprivation) and has
been since this index/measure was introduced.  He explained that this has
led to any retail businesses trying to survive, not only having to deal with
the decline of bricks and mortar retail due to the popularity and ease of
online shopping, but also the economic decline of the area which
successive governments have failed to address spanning back over 40
years.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 7 of 10
24. Mr Bond and Mr Roberts itemised other contributory factors which they felt
supported their case for a reduction in the RV ascribed to the subject
property:
25. Shop frontage – the property, a former HSBC bank, does not have the
traditional shop frontage which impacts upon attracting customers;
26. Council/Walk signage screens – one side of the property is obscured by
signage screens which block the general public viewing the one side of the
shop;
27. Market fast food outlet – during market days the one side of the shop is
obscured by a fast food outlet which has an impact on customers and
therefore trade;
28. Car parking multi storey – a multi storey car park is located at the bottom
end of the town which does not benefit businesses located at the top of the
town.  There are also problems with the lift which is regularly out of service;
29. Car parking town centre – there is limited town centre parking available and
as parking wardens now regularly patrol the area there is the increased risk
of a parking fine;
30. Since there is no back entrance to the subject property and as the Council
has marked the town centre with yellow lines, the Appellant runs the risk of
parking fines during loading/unloading goods to the appeal property;
31. Car parking at The Walk – situated opposite the subject property, The Walk
has changed ownership and is now chargeable;
32. Public transport – since 2018 Stagecoach has cut its bus services into
Ebbw Vale which has led to a decline in footfall of 60% and resulted in a
number of retail businesses struggling to survive. The Appellant had
contacted a number of organisations concerning this issue and was in the
process of running a petition;
33. Town centre regeneration – years of poor town centre planning and
refurbishment have resulted in Ebbw Vale town centre becoming a difficult
place for shoppers to visit and has resulted in a steady decline in footfall.
The Appellant had contacted his MP, AM’s and the Federation of Small
Businesses raising his concerns.  He had also found out that a number of
groups/working parties involved in regeneration have not delivered any
coherent strategy to help with the economic situation within Blaenau Gwent;
34. Public toilets - situated some 300 metres away and having only recently re-
opened, Mrs Roberts allowed visitors to the town to use the WC facilities in
the shop.
35. In addition, Mr Roberts and Mr Bond were also aware that a number of
national retailers will also be vacating their premises within the town in the
near future.

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 8 of 10
36. Store 21 was vacant for a considerable period, so has now been divided
into smaller units.  Mr Bond clarified that he has been offering shops at £50
per week but there has been no uptake.
37. To conclude, Mr Roberts reiterated that the appeal property does not lend
itself to a retail premises as the windows are high and narrow.
38. In response to questions, Mr Bond and Mr Roberts stated:
• As owner, Mr Bond does not want the ornamental porch area in the
property removed as it is very decorative and in-keeping with the
property.  Mr Roberts stated that the double doors also help with
keeping the heat in.  They did initially use this area to display goods
but these were stolen.
39. Both parties were given the opportunity to summarise their cases:
40. Mr Pearson informed the Tribunal that he had fully considered the
Appellants arguments.  The subject property had been re-measured and
he had considered a basket of rents and settlements from Bethcar Street
which supported £105m2 being ascribed.  In addition, he had taken into
account the non-traditional frontage and increased the allowance from
7.5% to 10% in line with a similar allowance ascribed to a comparable bank
in Market Street.  Any physical changes to the locality after the 1 April 2017,
the compilation date of the 2017 Rating List, would need to be addressed
by submitting a further proposal to the VOA.  He requested that the Tribunal
confirm a revised RV of £8,500 with effect from the 1 April 2017.
41. Mr Roberts thanked the Tribunal for listening to his case and explained that
he strongly believes that town centres should be re-generated as they form
part of a community.  He requested confirmation of £80m2 in line with other
properties within Bethcar Street.  Whilst he appreciated that the rent
payable may sound low, it is the amount that town centre traders can afford.
42. Mr Bond stated that he did not consider that non-domestic rates should be
payable whilst a property is being renovated.
43. At this point, Mr Pearson clarified that when a property is being renovated,
the taxpayer can approach the VOA to establish whether that property is
capable of beneficial occupation.

44. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Tribunal decided to reserve its decision.

Reasons for Decision

45. Having considered all the evidence placed before it the Tribunal decided as
follows:

46. In his proposal Mr Bond contended that the Rating List was inaccurate and
that the appeal property’s assessment should be reduced from £12,250 RV
to £8,000 RV with effect from the 1st April 2017.  However, at the hearing,

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 9 of 10
the Appellants considered that the RV should be reduced to circa £6,000
RV in line with the rent that Mr and Mrs Roberts are paying Mr Bond.

47. Mr Bond also maintained that the classification as a bank and premises
should be changed to a shop and premises, which the VO had agreed to
prior to the hearing.

48. Therefore, the only issue in dispute for the Tribunal to consider was the price
per m2 as applied by the VO to the property.  The VO had considered the
Appellants’ contentions and agreed that a reduction in the £m2 was
warranted from £140m2 to £105m2 and the non-standard frontage
allowance should be increased from 7.5% to 10% which equated to a
revised Rateable Value of £8,500 effective from the 1 April 2017.

49. However, the Appellants argued that the property should be valued in line
with larger shops located within close proximity to the subject property, 55
Bethcar Street at £85m2 and 32 Bethcar Street at £80m2.  They also
referred to a number of issues which they stated currently blight Ebbw Vale
town centre.

50. The Tribunal was aware that in accordance with relevant legislation the
appeal hereditament must be valued by having regard to values achieved
as at the Antecedent Valuation Date, the 1 April 2015, whilst looking at the
physical circumstances of the property as at the Material Day, the Compiled
List entry date of the 1 April 2017.

51. Whilst the Tribunal appreciated the current issues concerning Ebbw Vale
Town Centre as conveyed by Mr Bond and Mr Roberts, in relation to the
subject appeal it cannot have regard to any issues that have occurred after
the 1 April 2017.  The Members are aware that physical changes within a
locality may have an impact on the RV of a property and a proposal for a
reduction
in
assessment
because
of
a
“material
change
of
circumstances”(MCC) can submitted to the VOA in accordance with the
Non Domestic Rates  (Alteration of Lists and Appeals)(Wales) Regulations
2005 SI 758(W.63).  However, the issue of an MCC fell outside of the scope
of this particular appeal.

52. In accordance with principles outlined in Lotus and Delta v Culverwell (VO)
& Leicester City Council the rental evidence on the appeal property should
be taken as a starting point for the RV. However, the Tribunal was mindful
that the passing rent was effective from the 1 February 2018, nearly three
years after the Antecedent Valuation Date, and had no defined tenure or
terms.  Accordingly, the Tribunal attached little weight to this evidence.

53. The Tribunal considered a basket of rents and settlements from similarly
sized shops, ITMS, located on Bethcar Street in order to establish the
hypothetical rent for the appeal property as at the 1 April 2015.

54. The Members noted that the closest new letting to the AVD occurred on the
20 May 2014.  54 Bethcar Street, a traditional shop amongst a parade

Non-Domestic Rating Decision

Page 10 of 10
situated further along Bethcar Street, analysed to £110.09m2.  The VO
adopted £100m2.

55. Some two weeks later on the 1 June 2014, a further new letting was agreed
on another traditional shop and premises, 41 Bethcar Street.  This rent
analysed at £105.54m2 with the VO having adopted £160m2.

56. In addition, a rent review was agreed on 10/12 Bethcar Street, a bank and
premises with shop frontage, on the 20 August 2015, just under five months
after the AVD.  This rent analysed at £107.58m2.  It was noted that an
appeal submitted by a national firm of rating agents, CBRE, agreed a 10%
allowance for layout and frontage but the rate of £160m2 was not challenged
thereby appearing to suggest that the agent did not consider it to be
excessive.

57. With relation to those properties cited as comparable by the Appellants
namely, 55 Bethcar Street and 32 Bethcar Street, the Members agreed with
the VO that these properties were considerably larger than the subject
property, and as such, were not as comparable as the smaller properties
within Bethcar Street.

58. Therefore, whilst the Members sympathised with the Appellants regarding
the issues they raised concerning the current retail climate in Ebbw Vale,
from the evidence provided, they did not consider that the revised rate of
£105m2  proposed by the VO was excessive as it appeared to be in line
with other similar properties within Bethcar Street.

59. Consequently, in view of the above, the Tribunal determined that the
£105m2 adopted by Mr Pearson in his valuation of the appeal property was
fair and reasonable. With this in mind, the Tribunal confirmed the VO’s
revised assessment of £8,500 RV  with effect from the 1 April 2017 for Shop
and Premises 34 Bethcar Street, Ebbw Vale NP23 6HQ and allowed the
appeal in part.
